strengths: Significant Scalability Improvement: The paper successfully bridges the gap between hierarchical RL and modern high-throughput distributed RL, achieving a 25x to 240x throughput improvement compared to existing HRL baselines (HIRO, Option-Critic, MOC) on NLE.

Impressive Empirical Scale: Training and evaluating a hierarchical RL agent on 20 billion steps of experience on a highly complex, open-ended domain like NetHack is a landmark achievement for HRL, demonstrating positive scaling trends.

Elegant and Practical System Design: The three core design choices (single multi-head network, environment wrapper, and vectorized parallel V-trace implementation) are clean, highly practical, and easily integrable with modern asynchronous RL libraries like Sample Factory.

Thorough and Honest Evaluation: The paper includes excellent control baselines (e.g., flat APPO with mixed rewards, and SOL-HiPPO without intrinsic rewards) to clearly decouple the benefits of hierarchical structure from prior knowledge in the rewards.

Open Science and Reproducibility: Providing concrete PyTorch implementations of the parallelized V-trace operator in the appendix makes the systems contribution highly reproducible and directly useful for the community.
weaknesses: Dependence on Hand-crafted Intrinsic Rewards: The core method (SOL) relies on pre-specified intrinsic rewards for each option. When trained purely end-to-end with task rewards (the SOL-HiPPO variant), the performance is on par with flat baselines, indicating that the architecture still heavily relies on manual reward design to construct useful behaviors.

Fixed-step Option Termination: Options are executed for a fixed/sampled number of steps without a mechanism to dynamically interrupt execution based on sudden critical environment changes (such as low health in NetHack), which can lead to suboptimal policies.

strengths: Pioneering Scale in Hierarchical RL: The paper takes a major step in scaling Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) to the multi-billion frame regime (up to 20 billion steps on NetHack), which was previously computationally intractable.

Impressive Throughput Gains: The proposed Scalable Option Learning (SOL) achieves a 25x-240x speedup over existing HRL implementations, almost matching the throughput of highly optimized flat RL algorithms like APPO.

Excellent System Design: The combination of a single neural network with multiple heads, an environment wrapper tracking active policies, and a fully tensorized/parallelized batch V-trace calculation is elegant and practically highly useful.

Strong Empirical Results: Extensive evaluations across discrete roguelike environments (NetHack, MiniHack) and continuous control (PointMaze) demonstrate that SOL significantly outperforms flat baselines and state-of-the-art LLM-based exploration methods (Motif) when scaling up.
Reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, architectural descriptions, and actual PyTorch implementations for the parallelized V-trace and environment wrapper are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Dependency on Hand-Crafted Intrinsic Rewards: The success of SOL heavily relies on having access to pre-defined intrinsic reward functions $R_\omega$ for each option. As shown by the SOL-HiPPO baseline (which uses only the task reward), without these hand-crafted sub-rewards, the performance drops to the level of flat agents. This limits the autonomy of the agent in environments where sub-goals/rewards are not easily defined.

Minor Textual Discrepancy: The text contains a small contradiction regarding the maximum training steps on NetHack: Page 2 mentions '30 billion steps', whereas the abstract, main text of Section 5.2, and Figure 4 state '20 billion frames/steps'.

Sensitivity to Option Definition: It is unclear how sensitive the algorithm is to the choice of option reward scales and parameters (e.g., the execution lengths, reward coefficients in Table 3), which appear to require careful tuning across different environments.

strengths: Significant systems-level innovation addressing a major bottleneck in HRL: parallelizing trajectory collection and policy updates across heterogeneous options and execution lengths on GPU.
Unprecedented scale of HRL evaluation, training on the notoriously difficult NetHack environment for up to 20 billion steps, showing clear scaling benefits where flat RL baselines saturate.
Impressive throughput gains, achieving 25x to 240x higher steps-per-second compared to standard hierarchical baselines like HIRO, Option-Critic, and MOC.

Excellent presentation, clear mathematical formulation of the objectives, and strong reproducibility supported by concrete PyTorch code for the parallelized V-trace return computation in the appendix.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on hand-crafted intrinsic reward functions for each option. When these rewards are not provided (as in the SOL-HiPPO variant), the benefits of the hierarchy vanish, indicating that the system is not yet capable of end-to-end option discovery.

The option termination mechanism is simple and non-reactive: the option executes for a fixed number of steps chosen at invocation, lacking an online interruption mechanism to respond to sudden environmental changes.

strengths: Addresses a significant bottleneck in hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL): scaling online training to high-throughput systems and billions of frames of experience.
Outstanding systems-level engineering that achieves 35x to 580x higher throughput compared to prior deep HRL implementations, retaining 86% of the speed of a optimized flat RL agent.

Clean algorithmic design addressing non-stationarity and option degeneracy through a novel value bootstrapping mechanism at option switches, along with an adaptive exponential option execution length selection.

Exceptional empirical evaluation, running experiments up to 30 billion steps on the complex NetHack environment, establishing a new state of the art when combined with LLM-based reward synthesis (SOL+Motif).
Thorough ablations analyzing the importance of bootstrapping, option length selection, sensitivity to option count, and option reward scaling.
weaknesses: The primary experiments rely heavily on manually designed option rewards ($R_\omega$), such as Score and Health. While Section 5.3 demonstrates compatibility with unsupervised skill discovery (DIAYN), this is only showcased on simpler MiniHack tasks and has not yet been scaled to NetHack.

The GPU parallelization and batched transition mechanism are tightly coupled with the design choices of the Sample Factory framework, which may require significant effort to port to other distributed RL paradigms.

strengths: Significant Scaling Milestone: This work successfully scales online hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) to train on up to 30 billion frames of experience on the complex NetHack game. This is a massive scale compared to previous HRL studies which are typically limited to millions of steps.

Outstanding Throughput and Systems Engineering: Achieving a 35x to 580x speedup over existing hierarchical RL baselines (like HIRO, Option-Critic, and MOC) is a substantial systems achievement. Retaining 86% of the training throughput of a highly optimized flat PPO baseline makes online option-learning highly practical.

Algorithmic Novelty: The paper introduces a clean, sound approach to handle the mixture of option policies during training by bootstrapping option value functions upon option switches, combined with an adaptive option length selection mechanism.

Comprehensive Evaluation: The authors validate their approach on NetHack, MiniHack, and continuous control MuJoCo (G-maze) environments, demonstrating both discrete and continuous applicability. They also provide thorough ablations (e.g., regarding option length, scaling, and option quality) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Dependency on Pre-defined Option Rewards: A notable limitation is the reliance on prior knowledge in the form of pre-defined option reward functions (e.g., score, health, gold) to make the hierarchical division effective. While the integration with DIAYN in Section 5.3 shows compatibility with unsupervised reward synthesis, this is only tested on simpler MiniHack tasks and suffers from slower convergence.

Algorithmic Complexity of V-trace Implementation: The proposed parallelized V-trace with option switching requires custom Cython implementation and complex masking over batch segments. This might limit its immediate adoption and ease of integration into other deep RL libraries.

Small Option Cardinality: The empirical validation is restricted to settings with a very small number of options (typically 2 to 5). It is unclear how well the systems-level design scales if a task requires coordinating a large library of skills (e.g., dozens of options).

strengths: The paper successfully tackles a major bottleneck in hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL): the lack of computational scalability and throughput, achieving an impressive 35x to 580x speedup over existing hierarchical methods.

Excellent and rigorous empirical evaluation, training agents for up to 30 billion frames of experience on NetHack (NLE) and demonstrating clear scaling trends, as well as testing on MiniHack and continuous control (Gymnasium Robotics PointMaze).

Well-designed algorithmic details, such as the value bootstrapping mechanism upon option switches which permits stable optimization of independent option rewards under a mixed behavior policy, and the adaptive option execution length mechanism.
Comprehensive ablation studies covering option execution lengths, the number of option length bins, the quality/redundancy of options, and sample efficiency tradeoffs with multiple PPO epochs.
Highly reproducible with clear pseudocode, neural network architecture diagrams, and fully-specified PyTorch/V-Trace tensorized implementations in the appendix.
weaknesses: The method still relies on having either hand-defined option rewards (e.g., changes in score, health, gold, or velocity) or pairing with separate reward synthesis models (like DIAYN or Motif), which shifts some of the complexity to reward engineering.

The architectural design of using a shared network with a policy index embedding is conceptually similar to existing multi-task and conditioned RL architectures (e.g., Agent57), limiting the architectural novelty slightly, although its integration into a high-throughput options framework is novel.
